IRS Form 990 e-file · Schedule I Part II & 990-PF Part XV

Atlanta Food Flows

Food and cash moving between Atlanta-area food nonprofits, their partner agencies, and the national networks that supply them. Each line is a grant one organization reported giving another, valued as filed. How to read this

This page maps where food and the money behind it move among Atlanta-area food nonprofits. Everything on it is reconstructed from public filings. This note explains what each source contributes, how the pieces were joined, what was assumed, and where the picture is known to be incomplete. It is written for researchers and practitioners who want to use or check the figures. The Takeaways tab states what the recorded network shows under these definitions, with the metrics, the literature they draw on, and the hypotheses still to test.

What the map shows

Each line in the flow map is a grant that one organization reported giving to another: the giver's name, the recipient's name and usually its employer identification number, the cash amount, and the value of any noncash assistance such as food. Node size and ribbon width scale with dollars. Green is food (noncash), amber is cash. The map covers organizations in the Atlanta area, the outside organizations that supply or fund them, and the local agencies that receive from them. It is a map of reported transfers between organizations, not a census of all food moving through the region.

How the organization set was defined

"Atlanta-area food organizations" are tax-exempt organizations in the Business Master File whose ZIP code begins 300, 301, 302 or 303, and which either carry an NTEE code beginning with K (Food, Agriculture and Nutrition) or have a food-related word in their name (food, pantry, hunger, meals, kitchen, nutrition, feed, harvest, glean, grocer, farmers market). Labor unions matching "food" were removed. This yields organizations. The ZIP range is generous: it reaches Rome, Bremen and Newnan as well as the core metro. Organizations elsewhere enter the map only if they give to or receive from a member of this set.

How flows are built

  • A flow is one row of a giver's Schedule I Part II or 990-PF Part XV. The giver decides the value. For food, that is almost always fair market value, and the two largest givers here state the method as a wholesale average per pound.
  • Recipients are matched by EIN when the giver reports one. Private foundations report no EIN, so their recipients are matched by normalized name and may occasionally be missed or misjoined.
  • When an organization filed more than one return for the same year, the later one (an amended return) is kept.
  • "Latest filing per organization" shows each giver's most recent tax year, so a giver's flows are never double counted across years. Selecting a single year shows only returns for that tax year.
  • A grant an organization reports to its own EIN is shown as "direct distribution": food the organization handed out through its own programs rather than through a partner.
  • In the Sankey layout, the few flows between two distributors are drawn to a recipient-side copy of the receiving distributor, labeled "as recipient", so the columns stay in order. Organizations beyond the "Named per column" setting are grouped, recipients by city.
  • Audited USDA food received by a food bank is drawn as a flow from a single node, "USDA TEFAP commodities (via Georgia DHS)", using the most recent audit year.

An award is attributed to the federal fiscal year in which it started, using its total obligated amount. Sub-awards are attributed to the year of the sub-award date. "Traceable" federal money for an organization is the sum of awards made directly to it plus sub-awards naming it; most federal food money reaches nonprofits through the state, so this is a lower bound. Audited totals from Single Audits are the more complete figure where they exist.

The TEFAP layer

The Emergency Food Assistance Program is the largest federal food input to food banks and is absent from both of the other federal sources: the 990 folds USDA food into noncash contributions, and USAspending records almost no commodity awards. It is reconstructed from two ends.

  • USDA to Georgia. Entitlement food is allocated by a formula weighting poverty at 60% and unemployment at 40%; Georgia's index is about 3%. Bonus and Commodity Credit Corporation purchases, roughly twice the entitlement nationally, are not allocated by state table, so Georgia's share of those is shown as an estimate (national total times the index) and marked as such.
  • Georgia to food banks. Each food bank's Single Audit states the audited value of USDA food it received in its own fiscal year. Five of the seven contracted food banks report it; Second Harvest of Coastal Georgia reports only administrative funds, and Feeding the Valley files no Single Audit. The statewide sum is therefore a floor.
  • Reconciling the two. The audited sum runs several times USDA's entitlement figure. This is not an error: food banks value USDA food at the Feeding America national wholesale average per pound, while the entitlement is USDA's purchase cost and excludes bonus food. The two measure different things and are shown side by side, never added.
  • Separating food from cash in audits. The Clearinghouse records program names as auditors entered them, and one auditor books commodities under the administrative program number. Rows flagged as direct awards from USDA are treated as food and rows flagged as pass-through from the state as cash; 10.569 is always food.

The map

The Map layout places organizations at their addresses over census tracts of the 29-county Atlanta metropolitan area, with an optional shading of each tract's food access or income indicators. It is the view most likely to be misread, so its conventions are strict.

  • A point is a mailing address, not a service area. A pantry's tract says where its door is, not where its clients live. Regional redistributors and headquarters are the sharpest cases: a food bank in Gainesville receives food and sends it across north Georgia; a statewide charity receives at a Chamblee office for conferences elsewhere. The "Hide distributors" control removes organizations that themselves give food out, so that the remaining points are closer to the last recorded stop.
  • How points were placed. Organizations with a street address were geocoded by the Census Bureau's geocoder to coordinates and a census tract. Organizations with only a P.O. Box, or whose address could not be matched, are placed at the average position of matched organizations sharing their ZIP code, or failing that their city, and drawn hollow. Organizations without any Georgia address are not on the map.
  • What is not on the map, and why it matters. The largest single amounts have no destination point: food a distributor hands out through its own programs (reported as a grant to itself), the aggregate line for recipients under $5,000, and recipients named without an identification number. The note on the map states these for the current view. Because the missing recipients are disproportionately small pantries, an unshaded or empty tract can be a gap in reporting rather than a gap in service.
  • Shading and points measure different things and different years. The shading describes residents of a tract in 2010 to 2018; the points describe deliveries to organizations in 2022 to 2025. Placing one over the other invites a conclusion about mismatch between need and supply that the data cannot support. The map never computes food per resident, and readers should not either.
  • Dollars are the giver's valuation, not pounds or meals, and some large recipients are not pantries. A pet rescue that received food valued in the millions appears as a large circle. Hover or click to see what an organization is.
  • Religious congregations are a large share of recipients and serve members who may live elsewhere; 264 recipients have no organization type on record at all.
  • Restraint. Shading uses one sequential color, tracts are named by county and number, and the caveats stay on the canvas rather than in a footnote, so that a screenshot carries them.

Food security measures

  • Concentration: the share of all food given out by Atlanta-area organizations that passes through the single largest one, and the number of recipient agencies with only one recorded source.
  • Dependence: government grants as reported on an organization's own 990 (Part VIII line 1e, all levels of government) as a share of its total revenue, shown beside traceable federal awards and audited federal totals.
  • Where a cut lands: for each distributor with a funding base, exposure is that base divided by revenue (or, for the TEFAP base, audited USDA food divided by food given out), capped at one. A cut of c percent removes c × base from the distributor and is assumed to reduce each partner's food by c × exposure × that partner's current inflow. Results sum across distributors. This is arithmetic on reported figures, not a forecast.

Assumptions

  1. Reported grant values are taken at face value. Noncash food is valued by the giver, usually at a wholesale average per pound, and different givers use different rates.
  2. A giver's most recent return represents its current flows. Fiscal years differ between organizations, so "latest" mixes years ending between June 2023 and December 2025.
  3. Schedule I itemizes only recipients of $5,000 or more in a year. Smaller partners are absent, and an agency that appears to have one source may have several small ones.
  4. Organizations filing Form 990-EZ or 990-N report no grant detail, so they appear only as recipients even if they redistribute food.
  5. Recipient EINs are as reported by the giver. Name matching for foundation grants uses a normalized name and a prefix test.
  6. Federal awards are counted at obligation in their start year; spending may occur over several years.
  7. In the cut scenario, a distributor passes a funding loss to partners in proportion to current inflow and does not substitute other sources. Exposure is uniform across a distributor's partners.
  8. Georgia's share of bonus and CCC food is assumed proportional to its entitlement index. This is an estimate and is labeled as one.
  9. Audit years are used as reported. A June year end and a December year end in the same "audit year" cover different months.
  10. An organization's mailing address stands for its location. Approximate placements (P.O. Box ZIP or city) are marked but still plotted.
  11. The Atlanta metro is the 29-county metropolitan statistical area as defined by the Office of Management and Budget; organizations outside it are placed if they have Georgia addresses but fall outside the shaded frame.

Labels and technical notes

  • Atlanta food org (green): a member of the defined set. Outside supplier / funder (purple): any giver not in the set, including national food banks, foundations, donor-advised fund sponsors and the USDA pseudo-node. Partner agency (grey): a recipient not in the set and not a giver.
  • Food (noncash) is the giver's reported noncash assistance, whatever its description; on this map it is food in nearly every case. Cash is cash grants.
  • FY on a flow is the giver's tax year as filed. FY on a federal award is the federal fiscal year (October to September). Audit year is the year of the organization's fiscal year end.
  • Federal: nodes in the Sankey aggregate traceable awards by program group; they are not organizations.
  • Other outside givers, Other Atlanta distributors and Other recipients in [city] are groups created by the "Named per column" setting. Hover for the count.
  • (direct distribution) marks food an organization reported granting to itself. (as recipient) marks a distributor shown on the recipient side of the Sankey.
  • In view figures respect the current filters; the header totals do too.
  • Dollar amounts are rounded for display (K thousands, M millions, B billions). Tables in the side panel show exact reported values on hover.
  • EINs are shown as reported. Organizations named only by a foundation, with no EIN, are marked "EIN not reported".
  • On the map, filled points are street-geocoded, hollow points are approximate. Point size is dollars in and out under the current filters. Low income and low access is USDA's designation: a low-income tract where a significant share of residents live more than half a mile (urban) or ten miles (rural) from a supermarket. Quantitative shadings use five quantile classes over metro tracts.

Known gaps

  • Donors to an organization are not public. Schedule B is redacted in every public 990, so inflows are known only where the giver is itself a filer that itemizes grants.
  • Individual and direct corporate gifts never appear.
  • The Feeding America network's flows to other regions are outside the map; only the Atlanta-bound legs are included.
  • Two of Georgia's seven TEFAP food banks report no audited food value.
  • Sub-award reporting to USAspending is incomplete and capped per program.
  • Roughly one in eight dollars given by Atlanta-area organizations goes to a recipient that cannot be placed on the map.
